title: Govinda

teacherSummary.text: Old Govinda, still searching, comes to the ferry and asks for teaching. Siddhartha says that wisdom cannot be communicated in words, that every truth's opposite is also true, and that one must love the world. Asked to kiss Siddhartha's forehead, Govinda sees in his face a stream of countless faces and forms—the unity of all things—and bows, weeping, before his friend's smile.

answerKey.answer: His preference for things over ideas

Siddhartha believes that wisdom comes from living, not from thinking. The evidence is “he knew what is necessary just as well as Gotama, he was a perfect man, a saint” (Govinda, paragraph 15). In The Ferryman, Vasudeva says of himself: “All I’m able to do is to listen and to be godly, I have learned nothing else.” (The Ferryman, paragraph 29). Together the passages show that a simple listener can equal the Buddha.

Siddhartha has moved from cool detachment to love of the world. The evidence is “love, O Govinda, seems to me to be the most important thing of all” (Govinda, paragraph 30). In With the Childlike People, Kamala told him: “and yet you do not love me, you love nobody” (With the Childlike People, paragraph 46). Together the passages show that the man who could not love now calls love the highest thing.

Siddhartha sees Gotama’s whole life as an act of love. The evidence is “and yet loved people thus much, to use a long, laborious life only to help them, to teach them!” (Govinda, paragraph 32). In Gotama, the Buddha meets even a doubter “With half of a smile, with an unwavering openness and kindness” (Gotama, paragraph 41). Together the passages show that Gotama’s kindness, not his doctrine, proves his love.

Govinda’s search moves from taking refuge to admitting he has not found peace. In Gotama, “Govinda has heard the teachings, he has taken refuge in it.” (Gotama, paragraph 20). In Govinda, “the eternal search was visible in his look, eternal not-finding.” (Govinda, paragraph 37). A competing reading says Govinda failed by following a teacher. Yet his final vision comes through love for his friend, so his search is answered after all.

items.answerGuidance: Benevolently means in a kind, well-meaning way. Literally, Govinda sees Siddhartha’s face unchanged on the surface, the thousandfold depth closed again beneath it, as he smiles quietly and kindly (Govinda, paragraph 42).

items.text: What does “Govinda” suggest about the idea that wisdom cannot be taught? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: A stated inference (for example, that wisdom can only be shown, not told) backed by one located line, such as the one in Govinda, paragraph 41.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The chapter suggests wisdom can only be shown, not told. Support: Govinda gets no teaching he can keep, but sees the truth in the face he kisses (“which all came and disappeared, and yet all seemed to be there simultaneously” (Govinda, paragraph 41)).

items.text: Find one example of theme in this chapter. What does it reveal that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: Look for statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The stone (Govinda, paragraphs 22–26) carries the theme: Siddhartha loves the stone for what it is, which shows love of the world better than any statement.

items.text: How does the characterization in this chapter shape what we understand about the idea that wisdom cannot be taught?
items.lookFor: Look for what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Govinda is drawn as a lifelong searcher who cannot stop searching (“Never I’ll stop searching, this seems to be my destiny.” (Govinda, paragraph 4)); his searching is what keeps him from finding, as Siddhartha says in paragraph 7.

items.text: In the passage that begins “He came to the river and asked the old man to ferry him over, and when they got off the boat on the other side, he said to the old man: ‘You’re very good to us monks and pilgrims,…’”, why might Hesse have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Diction analysis of two words in the anchor passage.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: In Govinda, paragraph 2, the plain words of the request (“asked the old man to ferry him over”) hide who the ferryman is; the simple diction sets up the recognition scene.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Govinda”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: Old Govinda, still searching, comes to the ferry and asks for teaching. Siddhartha says that wisdom cannot be communicated in words, that every truth’s opposite is also true, and that one must love the world. Asked to kiss Siddhartha’s forehead, Govinda sees in his face a stream of countless faces and bows deeply.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The cause is Govinda’s last request for something to take away (Govinda, paragraphs 36–39). Effect: Siddhartha shows instead of tells, and Govinda finally sees.

items.text: How does “Govinda” build on “Om”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal or structural link between this and the previous chapter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Cause and effect: in “Om” Siddhartha reached serenity and took over the ferry; here that serenity is what draws Govinda, who hears of the wise old ferryman (paragraph 1).

items.text: What can we infer about a character's motives from what they say and do here, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: An inference about motive supported by a quoted line.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Govinda claims he wants a teaching, but what moves him is love (“drawn by great love and expectation” (Govinda, paragraph 40)); Siddhartha claims he has no teaching, yet he gives Govinda the vision.

items.text: The bell-ringer asked: “Govinda followed a teacher all his life; Siddhartha followed experience. Who learned more?” Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer anchored in the text.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A revised answer should contrast the outcomes: Govinda, the follower, still searches (paragraph 4), while Siddhartha, who followed no one, has found; and yet both meet in Gotama’s smile (paragraph 41).

items.text: Where does irony appear, and how does it connect this chapter to the larger concern with experience versus teaching?
items.lookFor: Look for gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The irony is that Govinda followed the Buddha all his life but finds the Buddha’s smile in the man who refused him (Govinda, paragraph 41).

items.text: Background: The ending echoes Buddhist ideas of non-self and the Hindu idea of the oneness of reality. How does knowing this change the way you read one moment in the chapter?
items.lookFor: A specific moment reread in light of the context.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Knowing the ideas of non-self and unity explains the vision: the faces are “still all Siddhartha” (Govinda, paragraph 41), so the self dissolves into all beings.

items.text: A critic might argue: “The final image, Siddhartha's smile resembling Gotama's, suggests he has found his own path to enlightenment.” How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the chapter.
items.lookFor: A defended position with evidence and one counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Agree: Siddhartha’s smile is “precisely the same” as Gotama’s (paragraph 41). A text counterpoint: Siddhartha himself says his words of love contradict Gotama’s, if only seemingly (paragraph 32).

items.text: Which character in this chapter acts most wisely, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: An evaluation using an explicit criterion and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: With love as the standard, Siddhartha is wisest (paragraphs 26, 30); Govinda least while he clings to searching (paragraph 4), though he is humble enough to ask.

items.text: Rewrite one moment of “Govinda” from the point of view of a different character. What does the new angle reveal or hide about the idea that wisdom cannot be taught?
items.lookFor: A rewrite that keeps the chapter’s events accurate, speaks in the chosen character’s voice, and ends with a sentence on what the new angle shows or hides.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Govinda’s view of the final scene (Govinda, paragraphs 40–43) is already the chapter’s angle; a version from Siddhartha’s side would show his calm and hide the overwhelming vision.

items.text: Write three questions of your own about “Govinda”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions at three levels, each answerable from the chapter, traded and answered with a line.
followUps: Which of your three questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Example set: recall, ‘What does Siddhartha pick up?’ (a stone, paragraph 22); why/how, ‘Why can’t wisdom be taught?’ (paragraph 19); what if, ‘Should Govinda stay at the river?’

items.text: Connect this chapter to the unity of all things: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Hesse need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment of thematic development across the work.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Strong and complete: the vision of all faces at once (Govinda, paragraph 41) is the unity the whole novel has pointed toward.

items.text: Is the theme in this chapter effective, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: An evaluative judgment with criteria and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Effective in the final image; some readers find Siddhartha’s long explanations (paragraphs 19–32) heavy before the vision shows the same thing.

items.text: Compare how “Govinda” treats the idea that wisdom cannot be taught with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Siddhartha see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A cross-text synthesis.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A comparison should name a story where a lesson is shown rather than told and quote “Knowledge can be conveyed, but not wisdom.” (Govinda, paragraph 19)

items.text: As the final chapter, does this ending resolve experience versus teaching? Argue whether the ending is earned.
items.lookFor: A prediction or judgment justified with textual clues.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Yes, in its own terms: the teacher-follower Govinda receives wisdom only by experience, a kiss and a vision (paragraphs 39–41); students can argue it stays open because Govinda cannot take it home in words.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of this chapter (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about the idea that wisdom cannot be taught?
items.lookFor: A modern setting, characters and conflict that keep the chapter’s core idea, with the one element that must not change named.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: A modern version keeps two old friends, one who followed a famous teacher and one who found his own way. What must stay is the final showing instead of telling (paragraph 41).

items.text: What question would you most like to ask Hermann Hesse about this chapter, and what answer do you think the text itself gives?
items.lookFor: A student-generated question answered from evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Example: ‘Did Govinda finally understand?’ The text shows tears and a deep bow (paragraph 43), so he felt what words could not give him.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

Integrate Emerson's "Brahma" with your reading of the vision, with attribution.

Explain Siddhartha’s claim that wisdom cannot be taught, the stone, and Govinda’s vision, using “wisdom cannot be passed on. Wisdom which a wise man tries to pass on to someone always sounds like foolishness.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, Govinda, para. 17), and compare one critical voice from this unit.

Apply a formal reading to Siddhartha’s claim that wisdom cannot be taught, the stone, and Govinda’s vision: show how imagery and repetition in “wisdom cannot be passed on. Wisdom which a wise man tries to pass on to someone always sounds like foolishness.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, Govinda, para. 17) build its meaning.

Argue how Siddhartha’s claim that wisdom cannot be taught, the stone, and Govinda’s vision advances the novel’s claim about teaching versus experience, testing “wisdom cannot be passed on. Wisdom which a wise man tries to pass on to someone always sounds like foolishness.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, Govinda, para. 17) against one earlier chapter.

Situate Siddhartha’s claim that wisdom cannot be taught, the stone, and Govinda’s vision within scholarship on Hesse and European representations of Indian thought, stating method and contribution, with “wisdom cannot be passed on.
